text: 8 PROGRAMS  ·  1,083 RELEASES  ·  441 CVEs  ·  OPENINTEL + REVERSE DNS

Does DNS software explain
when DNSSEC RFCs get adopted?

BIND 9, Unbound, NSD, Knot DNS, Knot Resolver, PowerDNS Auth/Recursor and OpenDNSSEC: when each one implemented an RFC, when it made it the default, when Ubuntu and Debian shipped that version, and which CVEs touched it -- lined up against what zones actually did in the OpenINTEL zone files and in reverse DNS.
Short version: code is never the wait; defaults do reach zones, through OS releases and only on newly signed zones, so they never show as a spike; one RFC was forced by validators before it was published; no CVE led a push.

8 projects cloned; 1,083 stable release dates from git tags (BIND development branches excluded). For each RFC: the first release that signs or validates it, the release that changed the default, and validator caps -- each backed by the commit and checked to be contained in the cited release.

the first Ubuntu LTS (16.04 to 24.04) and Debian (9 to 13) release carrying each version, from Launchpad and sources.debian.org: the path by which most operators actually receive a new default. The new-signings test is run around each OS release as well as around the upstream one.

441 CVEs across the eight products from NVD; 97 are DNSSEC mechanisms, classified by the mechanism the description names (NSEC3, validation, trust anchor, algorithm...) and attributed to a product only by NVD CPE.

OpenINTEL zone files for .se .nu .ch .li .ee .gov .fed.us (2016-06 to 2023-12) and reverse DNS for five RIRs (2009-03 to 2026-08), with the strict AFRINIC+ARIN panel for reverse shares and a per-delegation change ledger.

onset decomposition (RFC -> code -> first zone); event studies and a detrended release scan with a circular-shift null; a spike ledger naming what preceded every spike, against the chance rate; new signings vs rollovers; and the share of new reverse signings choosing each algorithm around every default change.
Code is never the wait; operators are

Across the algorithm and record-type RFCs the code lag runs -0.4 to +1.8 years (negative: a signer shipped it from the draft), while the lag from that release to the first zone runs 0.1 to 3.8 years. The RFC is never waiting for an implementation; it is waiting for an operator.
Defaults sit closer to take-off than RFCs do, but no event study or release scan finds a release month that moves the curve: after detrending, the smallest circular-shift p across the eight projects is 0.11. 97% of months in the release-scan span contain a stable release of one of the eight, so 'a release came just before' is always true and never evidence. Where defaults do show is in what newly signed zones choose, after the OS release that carries them (slide 5).
Verdict rule: FAST = first zone within a year of the RFC and 10% of signed delegations within four; SLOW = reached 10%, later; NEVER = under 1% of signed zones today.
Defaults changed in 2016; the zones moved in 2019 and 2021, by hand

Knot 2.1.0 (2016-01) and PowerDNS 4.0.0 (2016-07) made ECDSA the default; BIND 9.16.0 (2020-02) offered it as an opt-in policy. The first forward move, .se 2016-10 +17,193, is 3 months after the PowerDNS default but 10,748 of those zones were existing zones rolling over: an operator decision, not an update.
The moves that made ECDSA the majority were all rollovers, 30-35 months after any default (.se 2019-06..2019-07 +217,437). The .ch wave of 2021-06..2021-11 (+591,333) was new signings choosing ECDSA 96% of the time -- that is where a default acts: silently, on new zones, years after it changed. 2 of 31 spikes sit within 3 months of a default, against a 9% chance rate.
Updates work: the OS release is the event, and it acts on new zones only

An update cannot roll an existing zone; it can only change what a zone signed after the update gets. So the test is the share of NEW signings choosing the algorithm, which the reverse ledger records per delegation.
ECDSA: on their upstream dates the 2016 Knot and PowerDNS defaults left no trace (0.2% -> 0.3%, 0.3% -> 0.2%), and neither did Ubuntu 16.04, which carried only Knot. Debian 9 (2017-06-17) was the first OS release to ship both ECDSA-default signers: in the year after it, 57.1% of new reverse signings chose ECDSA (0.2% the year before), from 55 blocks (3 before). A second step, 22.8% -> 38.8%, came with BIND 9.16.0 in Ubuntu 20.04 and Debian 11.
RSA/SHA-256: new signings choosing it went 0.9% -> 20.0% across OpenDNSSEC 1.2.0's default (2011-03) and kept rising for two years; BIND 9.7.0 had shipped it 13 months earlier, so it reads as availability, not one vendor.
EdDSA: never a default anywhere; 14 rollovers to it in the whole ledger; two forward episodes, both withdrawn. No default, no adoption.
The one vendor-triggered case, and it happened before the RFC

Names with 100 or more NSEC3 iterations collapsed in 2021-10..2021-11 in every TLD that had them (.nu 12,145 -> 110), 10 months before RFC 9276. Two to three months earlier PowerDNS 4.5.0 and Unbound 1.13.2 had capped iterations, and CVE-2021-40083 (Knot Resolver, assertion failure on NSEC3 with too many iterations) was published.
All 3 spikes are within 3 months of a cap against a 14% chance rate. The caps and the CVE are one event: resolver vendors agreed to reject high counts and the zones that would have failed were re-signed. The RFC codified what validators had already forced. BIND's own default change (100 -> 10) was 140 months earlier and moved nothing.
CVEs follow deployment; none led a push

97 of the 441 CVEs are DNSSEC mechanisms; 69 of those sit in the RFC 4033/4034/4035 core (validation, RRSIG, DNSKEY, NSEC) and belong to no single later RFC. The per-RFC sets are small: NSEC3 12, trust anchors 8, ECDSA 2, EdDSA 1, RSA/SHA-256 and CDS none.
A CVE is attached to an RFC by the mechanism its description names, not by citing the RFC: 6 of the 97 DNSSEC CVEs cite any RFC in their text, and only 2 cite one of the RFCs studied here (CVE-2013-4854 -> RFC 5011; CVE-2023-50868 -> RFC 5155, 9276).
Every CVE nearest to an adoption spike is a validator bug (memory leak, assertion failure). Median lag from a spike to the nearest CVE: 16 months for ECDSA, 57 for NSEC3. CVE-2022-38178 came 4 months before the second EdDSA episode; it is a BIND memory leak and not a reason to sign with EdDSA.
The one CVE inside a causal chain is CVE-2021-40083: a symptom of the iteration problem the 2021 caps fixed, published the month the caps shipped. The DNSSEC CVE surface is on validators (Unbound, BIND, Knot Resolver, PowerDNS Recursor); the signers whose defaults move zones publish almost none.
NSEC3 order of events: BIND 9.6.0 signs it 2008-12, the first NSEC3-signed reverse delegations appear 2009-07, the first CVE 2009-10. Code, then deployment, then CVEs, each within a year.
SO WHY FAST, SLOW OR NEVER
How a change reaches a zone decides its speed

Fast RFCs are the ones a signer default carries into every newly signed zone. Slow ones need operators to roll existing zones, and operators do that in six-figure batches years after the default changed. Never-adopted ones had no default anywhere. The only RFC that moved on a vendor's schedule was the one where validators refused the old value.
signer default, inherited by new zones
first zone 2010-03; new reverse signings 0.9% -> 20.0% across the 2011 default
signer defaults reach new zones via Debian 9 (2017); majority by operator rollovers
first zone 2015-11; majority only via 2019 rollovers and the 2021 .ch wave
collapse 2021-10, ten months before the RFC
only useful where the parent acts on it
never a default; Russian namespace not in corpora

Which software signs a zone is never visible from its records; 'nearest release' is timing evidence. Registry and registrar signing platforms are closed source and are not in the release list.
OpenINTEL here is monthly aggregates for seven TLDs from 2016-06 (2020-05 for .ch/.li) to 2023-12, so RSA/SHA-256 and NSEC3 adoption are visible only in reverse DNS, and forward spikes cannot be attributed to an operator.
Reverse DNS is small (25,930 change events on 13,654 delegations) and NSEC3 is visible there only through algorithm 7.
OS package dates bound when a default became reachable by apt, not when anyone upgraded. The Debian 9 step rests on 55 blocks in one corpus, APNIC-heavy, with one block a third of it.
With 3 to 31 spikes per RFC, 'beats chance' is a reading, not a test with a p-value. CVE attribution is by NVD product only.
Decks with every figure and ledger: dnssec_rfc_why.pptx (per-RFC timelines), dnssec_program_rfc_cases.pptx (per-program case studies), dnssec_algorithm_flows.pptx (what zones move between). CSVs: dns_software_*.csv, dns_cve_list.csv, dns_program_rfc_spikes.csv.
